Why Gemma 2's Sliding Window Attention Is an Engineering Win

Google's Gemma 2 release introduces a compelling hardware-aware architectural choice: alternating between local sliding-window attention and standard global self-attention across layers. In standard attention, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length, consuming multiple gigabytes of VRAM on long documents. By restricting half of the layers to a local sliding window (e.g. 4096 tokens), Gemma 2 cuts KV cache memory consumption by approximately 50% without degrading downstream perplexity on long-context tasks. This makes running the 2B model on low-end edge devices and standard RAM truly viable.

Concept of the Day: Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes

When distributing keys across a cluster of database or cache nodes, standard modulo hashing (hash(key) % N) causes a devastating cache invalidation storm whenever a node is added or removed. Consistent hashing maps both servers and data keys to a circular 360-degree hash ring. When a server departs, only the keys immediately following it on the ring need relocation. By assigning dozens of "virtual nodes" to each physical machine, consistent hashing eliminates uneven key distribution and prevents single-node hotspots during scale-out events.
